solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Merit of French verse in translation (7)

indicatorNotes.in translation: translating turns words into new forms, so the letters of VERSE are rendered anew

annotation.surface: A critic weighing the worth of some French poetry once it has been translated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of French' is a common crossword way of asking for the French word for 'of'.
annotation.definitionFit: To deserve something is to merit it; both are verbs.

entries.clue: Let down — initially dud is assigned to position (12)

annotation.surface: A dud employee being given a job, to everyone's dismay.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a complaint about a bad hire, but 'Let down' is the definition, as an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe the feeling when hopes or expectations have not been met.

entries.clue: Quiet, more mature, say, accepting you assume responsibility (8)

indicatorNotes.say: marks OLDER as one example of 'more mature'
indicatorNotes.accepting: to accept something is to take it in, so OLDER takes U into its middle

blocks.note: U = you, as in text speak

annotation.surface: Advice to someone quiet and growing up: time to take charge.
annotation.walkthrough: U sits inside OLDER after the O, giving O-U-LDER.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: carrying a load on your shoulders pictures taking on a duty.

entries.clue: Castigate pace of progress (4)

blocks.note: an old verb meaning to scold severely, kept alive in a longer word beginning BE-
speed, as in miles per hour

annotation.surface: A boss scolding a team for the slow speed of its work.
annotation.walkthrough: The scolding sense of RATE survives mainly in 'berate'.
annotation.definitionFit: Rate means both to scold severely and a speed of progress.

entries.clue: Tirade supports former monarch going off the rails (6)

indicatorNotes.supports: in a down clue, RANT sits below ER, holding it up

blocks.note: ER = Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen

annotation.surface: A king ousted from the throne ranting as he loses his grip.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supports' is a down-clue convention: the supporting piece sits underneath, so it comes second.
annotation.definitionFit: Errant means straying from proper conduct, which is going off the rails.

entries.clue: Highly praise guile so easily at start — out of order! (8)

indicatorNotes.out of order: the letters are put in a different order

annotation.surface: An objection that praising someone's cunning so readily is improper.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation reads like a chairman's ruling, but it is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the Greek for 'good words', often spoken of the dead at a funeral.

entries.clue: Sovereign relations good (4)

annotation.surface: A monarch on friendly terms with his family or neighbours.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sovereign relations' reads as diplomacy, but the definition is 'Sovereign' alone.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a male ruling monarch is one kind of sovereign, alongside a queen.

entries.clue: Mundane way to welcome home? (7)

indicatorNotes.to welcome: ROUTE takes IN inside it, as a host welcomes a guest in

annotation.surface: Asking what the everyday way is to greet someone arriving home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Home' gives IN, as in 'staying in' for staying at home; the question mark flags that stretch.
annotation.definitionFit: Routine as an adjective means ordinary or mundane.

entries.clue: Business person found in daycentre pre neurosurgery (12)

indicatorNotes.found in: the answer is found inside the next words

blocks.note: the letters run on from after DAYC to before OSURGERY, across three words

annotation.surface: A businessman spotted at a day centre before his brain surgery.
annotation.walkthrough: The odd 'pre' is the giveaway that the letters matter more than the sense.
annotation.definitionFit: An entrepreneur is a person who starts businesses.

entries.clue: Transport Glaswegian maybe carrying duck — I’m not sure! (7)

indicatorNotes.maybe: a Glaswegian is one example of a SCOT
indicatorNotes.carrying: one who carries something holds it within, so SCOT holds O inside

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nought in cricket, shaped like O

annotation.surface: Someone from Glasgow hauling a duck around and unsure what to make of it.
annotation.walkthrough: Duck for O comes from cricket, where a batsman out for nothing scores a duck.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the two-wheeled vehicle, motorised or kicked along, is one form of transport.

entries.clue: In middle of a maiden song, terribly tense (7)

indicatorNotes.terribly: SONG is mangled terribly into a new order

blocks.note: M = maiden, a cricket over with no runs

annotation.surface: A singer growing anxious midway through a young woman's ballad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In middle of' looks like a container instruction, but it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Amongst means in the middle of, both prepositions.

entries.clue: Part of Papal Mass this Sunday? (4)

annotation.definitionNote: PALM names the Sunday: the definition asks which word goes before 'Sunday'

indicatorNotes.Part of: the answer is a part of the words that follow

blocks.note: the last three letters of the first word plus the first letter of the second

annotation.surface: A question about the Pope's Mass on a particular Sunday.
annotation.walkthrough: Palm Sunday, the Sunday before Easter, suits a Papal Mass, so the whole clue hangs together.
annotation.definitionFit: Palm Sunday is the Sunday a Papal Mass might mark.

entries.clue: Quality of thanks recalled: statement of admiration (9)

indicatorNotes.recalled: TA is called back, so it runs the other way

blocks.note: ta is British slang for thanks

annotation.surface: Remembering the grace with which someone said thank you, in a speech of praise.
annotation.walkthrough: TA is informal British for 'thank you'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a characteristic trait someone or something has.

entries.clue: A constant trade union supporter in fact (8)

blocks.note: c is the constant for the speed of light

annotation.surface: A loyal backer of the union movement, really.
annotation.walkthrough: C for constant comes from physics, where c is the speed of light; the definition hides at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: Actually means in fact; both work as adverbs.

entries.clue: Describing this turn made surprisingly? (8)

indicatorNotes.surprisingly: the letters end up somewhere surprising

annotation.surface: Commenting on an unexpected twist that has just taken place.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a turn made surprisingly is one never imagined, which is what UNDREAMT describes.
annotation.definitionFit: Undreamt (of) means never imagined, fitting a surprising turn.

entries.clue: Angry at outset is returning rather inferior furniture item (9)

indicatorNotes.at outset: takes the letter at the outset of each of the next four words

blocks.note: first letters of is, returning, rather, inferior

annotation.surface: A customer cross about sending back a second-rate piece of furniture.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Returning' looks like a reversal signal, but it only supplies its first letter R.
annotation.definitionFit: Irritable means easily angered, cross.

entries.clue: Device to remind social gathering agent’s coming up (6)

indicatorNotes.coming up: in a down clue, REP goes upward, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: a bee is a gathering, as in a spelling bee or sewing bee
a rep is a sales agent

annotation.surface: A gadget pinging to tell you that the party with your agent is coming soon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Agent's' is 'agent is', so REP is what comes up.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a pager or alarm that emits a sound to alert its wearer.

entries.clue: Release charge about right (4)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' can mean around, so FEE is placed around R

annotation.surface: A lawyer saying the case against a prisoner is correct, or that they should go.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charge' suggests an accusation, but here it is a price.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: letting a captive go, both verbs.

entries.clue: Seven years at the coalface — finally moan constantly, effective at first (7)

indicatorNotes.finally: takes the final letter of each of 'at the coalface'

blocks.note: last letters of at, the, coalface
to nag is to moan constantly

annotation.surface: A miner complaining endlessly after seven years underground.
annotation.walkthrough: The teenage years run from thirteen to nineteen, seven in all; the mining surface hides that.
annotation.definitionFit: The teenage years, thirteen to nineteen, are seven years of life.
annotation.definitionNote: TEENAGE is an adjective or collective name for the seven teen years

entries.clue: Diplomat ignoring Oscar’s resentment (4)

indicatorNotes.ignoring: to ignore something is to leave it out of account, so the O is dropped from the diplomat

blocks.note: Oscar is O in the phonetic alphabet; removed

annotation.surface: An ambassador resentful at not winning an Oscar.
annotation.walkthrough: Oscar here is not the film award but the NATO phonetic alphabet word for the letter O.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: grudging discontent at another's luck or possessions.

entries.clue: Unhappy Tory (4)

blocks.note: sad, low in spirits, a colour word for mood
the Conservative party's colour, standing for its members

annotation.surface: A glum Conservative politician.
annotation.walkthrough: Tory is the nickname for Britain's Conservative party, whose colour is blue.
annotation.definitionFit: Blue means both sad and Conservative in British politics.

entries.clue: Looting — small community needs new start (7)

annotation.definitionNote: Looting is a noun here, like PILLAGE

indicatorNotes.needs new start: the first letter of VILLAGE is swapped for a different one

blocks.note: a village is a small community; its V is replaced by P

annotation.surface: A plundered hamlet that has to rebuild from scratch.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue does not say which new letter; with -ILLAGE and the definition, only P works.
annotation.definitionFit: Pillage is looting, taking goods by force.

entries.clue: Reveal most of ugly dive has to be revamped (7)

indicatorNotes.most of: take UGLY without its last letter
indicatorNotes.to be revamped: the letters are remade in a new order

annotation.surface: A seedy bar that needs doing up, with its unattractive side exposed.
annotation.walkthrough: A dive is a seedy bar, which is why it needs revamping in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: making known something previously private, both verbs.

entries.clue: Tenant perhaps, full of energy, to go in again (2-5)

indicatorNotes.full of: something full of a thing has it inside, so the tenant word holds E within

blocks.note: a tenant is one example of a renter

annotation.surface: A lively tenant moving back into a flat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks a tenant as one example of the wider word; the E goes in after its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: The prefix RE- means again and ENTER means go in, so the parts spell out the definition.
